analysis.one_liner: Lets group health plans impose benefit limits if they are spelled out and disclosed before enrollment.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 422–3 with near-total bipartisan agreement, but the Senate committee it went to never acted, and the bill expired at the end of the Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law bars group health plans from treating similarly situated enrollees differently through limits or restrictions on benefits. This bill creates an exception: a plan can impose such limits if they are explicit, are given to the employer in writing before the sale, and are described to workers in plain language before they enroll and again at enrollment. It passed the House almost unanimously in March 2009, went to a Senate committee, and never came out.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers and employers offering group coverage gain legal certainty: once limits on benefits are written and disclosed, they cannot be attacked as discrimination under the existing rules. Workers and their families gain advance, plain-language notice of what their plan will not pay for, rather than finding out at the pharmacy or the hospital.

how_it_helps.text: Requires that any limits or restrictions on benefits be 'explicit and clear' and be disclosed to the employer in writing before the coverage is sold.
Requires the employer and insurer to give participants a description of the limits, 'in a form that is easily understandable,' before they enroll and again at enrollment.

Removes legal ambiguity by excluding disclosed limits from the federal prohibition on restrictions on benefits for similarly situated individuals under ERISA, the Public Health Service Act, and the Internal Revenue Code.

analysis.who_pays: Enrollees who hit the newly explicit limits. Disclosure tells a worker what the plan will not cover; it does not cover it. The bill also converts what had been a blanket prohibition into something a plan can lawfully do, so workers trade a rule they could invoke against restrictive coverage for a notice they can only read.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers who hit newly spelled-out benefit caps

drawbacks.text: The bill makes benefit limits expressly lawful so long as they are disclosed, so disclosure replaces protection: a worker can read a plain-language description of a cap but can no longer argue the cap itself violates the nondiscrimination rules for similarly situated individuals.
The 'easily understandable' description comes before enrollment in an employer-chosen plan; a worker whose only coverage options all contain the same limits gains notice but no real choice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the disclosure requirement is a genuine, if modest, gain: knowing before you enroll that a plan caps a benefit is better than discovering it later. The cost is that the bill converts those caps from a potential violation into an expressly permitted practice. Both effects are real but modest; the bill is more a litigation-avoidance measure for plans and insurers than a consumer-protection measure, and it died in the Senate, so neither effect ever took hold.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 422–3, then it went to the Senate's Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on March 3, 2009 by Rep. Michael Burgess, it was marked up and ordered reported by the Energy and Commerce subcommittee and committee the very next day by voice vote.

It was reported on March 30, 2009, considered under suspension of the rules (a fast track reserved for noncontroversial bills), and passed 422–3 the next day, with 249 of 253 Democrats and 173 of 178 Republicans voting yes.

The Senate received it on April 1, 2009 and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where no further action was recorded before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one changed the law. Because the bill died, the existing prohibition on undisclosed benefit limits stayed exactly as it was, and plans and insurers never received the safe harbor they sought; workers neither gained the promised disclosures nor lost the existing rule.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody — the status quo stayed in place

for.name: Rep. Michael C. Burgess
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through the House in its first month.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.role: House Energy and Commerce Committee member who moved passage
for.what_they_did: Moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill, bringing it to the House floor within a month of introduction.

for.name: 422 House members
for.what_they_did: Passed the bill 422–3 under suspension of the rules.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral on April 1, 2009 and never reported it, keeping it off the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was nearly unanimous across both parties: 249 of 253 Democrats and 173 of 178 Republicans voted yes, with only 3 members voting no.

industries.note: The bill gives insurers a safe harbor to impose explicit caps on benefits without facing challenges under the federal nondiscrimination rules, in exchange for new plain-language disclosure duties. Consumers get advance notice of the caps, but the caps themselves become expressly lawful.
Plan sponsors gain the same legal certainty plus clearer rules, but take on the paperwork of disclosing limits to workers before and at enrollment.
